# Angular

Angular templates: highlighting of bindings, pipes and control flow blocks, and the Angular language server with errors, completion, hover and navigation between templates and components.

## Files

- **Angular Template**: `*.component.html`. An Angular template is HTML by its extension, so Flux tells it apart by the name the Angular style guide gave templates before version 20; a template named otherwise (`app.html` next to `app.ts`) opens as HTML.

## Language servers

Flux starts the server when a file of the language opens. If it isn't on the machine, Flux
installs it into `~/Library/Application Support/flux/servers` (Settings → Language Servers shows
where each one comes from, and installs, updates or removes it).

- **ngserver** (the npm package `@angular/language-server`, with TypeScript and Angular's language service) — with a Node.js of Flux's own. It takes TypeScript and Angular's language service from the project when it has them, otherwise the ones installed with it. It serves the templates; the TypeScript of components stays with the TypeScript server.

## Highlighting

- [tree-sitter-angular](https://github.com/dlvandenberg/tree-sitter-angular) v0.9.2, MIT — the grammar and its highlighting query, adapted to Flux's theme scopes (`licenses/`). The grammar reads Angular's expressions itself: bindings (`[prop]`, `(event)`, `[(ngModel)]`), `{{ }}` with pipes, structural directives (`*ngFor`), `@if`, `@for`, `@switch`, `@defer` and `@let`, ICU messages.
- `<style>` and `style="…"` are highlighted as CSS, `<script>` as JavaScript. Needs Flux 0.4 or later.

# Classic Themes

Classic Dark and Classic Light for Flux: calm color schemes — warm gray and white — on Flux's frosted
glass. The two themes are a pair: choose them as the dark and the light theme of **Settings →
Appearance → Theme → Sync with OS**, and Flux follows macOS between them.

- **Classic Dark** — warm gray neutrals. Code: keywords, commas and semicolons orange, strings green,
  numbers blue, functions yellow, fields and constants purple (constants in italics), annotations
  olive, doc comments green italic.
- **Classic Light** — white islands on pale gray. Code: keywords dark blue, strings green, numbers
  blue, function declarations teal, fields and constants purple, annotations olive, comments gray
  italic.
- In both, plain identifiers and types keep the text color; selection, focus, changed files and diffs
  use the scheme's own colors, and the terminal has a matching ANSI table.

Version 0.2 gave the themes these names: a Flux that had one of them chosen under its former name
keeps it.

# Dotenv

.env files: highlighting of keys, values, references and comments, and checks — keys set twice, files with values Git doesn't ignore, keys missing from .env.example.

## Files

- **Dotenv**: `.env`, `.env.*` (`.env.local`, `.env.production`, `.env.example`), `*.env` (`production.env`). Needs Flux 0.4 or later.

## Highlighting

`KEY=value` and `export KEY=value`; values unquoted, in double quotes (over several lines, with escapes like `\n` and references), in single quotes or backticks (as they are); references to other variables — `$NAME`, `${NAME}`, `${NAME:-default}` — in double quotes and unquoted values; `# comments`, after a value too. Values are read as the `dotenv` package of Node.js reads them: an unquoted value ends at a `#`.

- The grammar is written for the catalog — [`grammars/tree-sitter-dotenv`](https://github.com/egor4geev/flux-plugins/tree/main/grammars/tree-sitter-dotenv), MIT — and so is the highlighting query (`licenses/`).

## Checks

The plugin's problems show as a language server's do: underlined, on hover, in the Problems window (F2) — for the open files as they are typed, for the project's other `.env` files as they are on disk (the project's folder and two levels below it, without `node_modules`).

- **A key set twice** — a warning on the later lines. The `dotenv` package keeps the first value, a shell the last one.
- **A file Git doesn't ignore** — a warning on its first line, when the file has values: the next commit may take it. A file Git already has gets a warning too. Templates — `.env.example`, `.env.sample`, `.env.template`, `.env.dist`, `example.env` — are meant to be committed and are not checked. Some frameworks keep defaults in a committed `.env`: turn the check off in Settings → Plugins → Dotenv.
- **A file against its template** — hints: the keys of `.env.example` (or `.env.sample`, `.env.template`) of the same folder that a file doesn't set, on its first line; the keys a file sets that the template doesn't list, on their lines.

## Permissions

- **The project's files, to read**: the `.env` files and their templates.
- **Programs: `git`**: `git check-ignore` and `git ls-files` tell which `.env` files Git ignores and which it has. Without Git, or outside a repository, this check is skipped.

plugins.name: ESLint
plugins.description: ESLint in Flux: the problems of the project's ESLint rules as you type, and their quick fixes — fix a problem, all of its kind, or turn the rule off for a line.
plugins.manifest:
# ESLint for Flux: a language server of the catalog, for the files of the languages other plugins
# bring (JavaScript and TypeScript, Vue, Svelte, Astro).
#
# Plugin API 0.4: it needs a Flux that pulls a server's problems (`textDocument/diagnostic`: this
# server publishes none); a secondary server — never a file's main one (by the plugins' order
# "ESLint" comes before "Svelte" and "Vue") — that starts only in projects with ESLint.
id = "flux.eslint"
name = "ESLint"
version = "0.1.0"
api = "0.4"
authors = ["Egor Ageev"]
description = "ESLint in Flux: the problems of the project's ESLint rules as you type, and their quick fixes — fix a problem, all of its kind, or turn the rule off for a line."
repository = "https://github.com/egor4geev/flux-plugins"
icon = "icons/eslint.svg"

# The server runs the project's own ESLint (`node_modules/eslint`). It starts in a project with an
# ESLint config — flat (`eslint.config.*`, ESLint 9 and later) or legacy (`.eslintrc*`) — in the root
# or next to the file's `package.json`, or with `eslint` among that `package.json`'s dependencies.
[[language-servers]]
id = "vscode-eslint-language-server"
command = "vscode-eslint-language-server"
args = ["--stdio"]
languages = ["javascript", "jsx", "typescript", "tsx", "vue", "svelte", "astro"]
install = { npm = ["vscode-langservers-extracted"], bin = "vscode-eslint-language-server" }
secondary = true
activation = { files = ["eslint.config.*", ".eslintrc*"], dependencies = ["eslint"] }

# The server asks for the whole configuration of each document (`workspace/configuration` with
# the section ""): these keys are its answer, and it reads each of them — none may be missing.
# - `validate = "on"`: every file it gets is linted; ESLint 9's flat config skips the files no
#   config object matches (`.vue` without a Vue plugin) silently, `onIgnoredFiles = "off"`.
# - `useFlatConfig` is left out: ESLint 9 and later read `eslint.config.*`, 8.57 reads it when
#   there is one, older versions `.eslintrc.*`. `experimental.useFlatConfig` is the old switch
#   of ESLint 8.21–8.56, off.
# - `workspaceFolder`: the project's root (`{ uri, name }`, as the server's own client sends it):
#   a relative `nodePath` and the working directory fall back to it.
# - `workingDirectory.mode = "auto"`: ESLint runs in the folder of the file's nearest
#   `package.json` or config — each package of a monorepo with its own config.
# - `nodePath = ""`: ESLint is looked up from the file's folder; `format = false`: formatting
#   stays with the formatter; the documentation action is off — it opens a page Flux doesn't show.
[language-servers.settings]
validate = "on"
run = "onType"
packageManager = "npm"
useESLintClass = false
nodePath = ""
quiet = false

# ESLint

ESLint in Flux: the problems of the project's ESLint rules as you type, and their quick fixes — fix a problem, all of its kind, or turn the rule off for a line.

## Files

The files of JavaScript and TypeScript (with JSX), Vue, Svelte and Astro — the languages their own plugins bring. A file is checked when the project's ESLint config covers it: Vue, Svelte and Astro files need the config's plugin for them.

## Language servers

Flux starts the server when a file of these languages opens in a project with ESLint: an `eslint.config.*` (ESLint 9 and later) or `.eslintrc*` config in the project's root or next to the file's `package.json`, or `eslint` among that `package.json`'s dependencies. It runs next to the language's own server and never takes its place. The problems are checked as you type, a moment after you stop. If it isn't on the machine, Flux installs it into `~/Library/Application Support/flux/servers` (Settings → Language Servers shows where each one comes from, and installs, updates or removes it).

- **vscode-eslint-language-server** (the npm package `vscode-langservers-extracted`) — with a Node.js of Flux's own. It runs the project's own ESLint (`npm install` first) in the folder of the file's nearest `package.json` or config — each package of a monorepo with its own. Quick fixes (⌥↵): fix this problem, fix all of the rule's problems, fix everything that can be fixed, turn the rule off for this line or the file. Needs Flux 0.4 or later.
- With an `.eslintrc.*` config (ESLint 8 and older) every file of these languages is checked: a Vue, Svelte or Astro file without the config's plugin for it shows a parsing error. With `"settings": { "validate": "probe" }` of the server (Settings → Language Servers → the server → Configure…) only the files the config has a parser for are checked.

# Flux Tiles

File icons as colored tiles: each kind of file gets Flux's own glyph in white (near-black where
white wouldn't read) on a rounded tile of its color — Rust orange, TypeScript blue, Python blue
with a yellow snake, Go cyan, Docker blue, licenses gold. The tiles are full-color, so they look the
same on light and dark themes.

The set knows the same files as Flux Icons, the set Flux comes with. Folders keep Flux's own icons;
a file the set doesn't know gets a gray tile, unless its language plugin brings an icon of its own.

`icons/` and `icon-themes/tiles.toml` (edit the script, not the generated files).

# Python

Python: highlighting, Pyright (types, completion, navigation, the project's virtual environment) and Ruff (linting and formatting).

## Files

- **Python**: `*.py`, `*.pyi`, `*.pyw`.

## Language servers

Flux starts the server when a file of the language opens. If it isn't on the machine, Flux
installs it into `~/Library/Application Support/flux/servers` (Settings → Language Servers shows
where each one comes from, and installs, updates or removes it).

- **Pyright** — from npm, with a Node.js of Flux's own. It uses the project's virtual environment (`.venv`, `venv` or `env` with a `pyvenv.cfg`, otherwise `$VIRTUAL_ENV`).
- **Ruff** — the latest release from GitHub (checked by its `.sha256`): linting and formatting (⌥⌘L).

## Highlighting

- The grammar and its highlighting query: [tree-sitter-python](https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-python) v0.25.0, MIT — `licenses/`.

plugins.description: Tailwind CSS in Flux: completion of classes with the CSS they make, the CSS of a class on hover, errors in classes and in Tailwind's at-rules, and their quick fixes — from the Tailwind CSS language server.
plugins.manifest:
# Tailwind CSS for Flux: a language server of the catalog, for the files of the languages other
# plugins bring (HTML, CSS, JavaScript and TypeScript, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Angular templates).
#
# Plugin API 0.4: a secondary server — never a file's main one (by the plugins' order "Tailwind CSS"
# comes before "Vue"), its class completion and hover joining the main server's — that starts only
# in projects with Tailwind CSS.
id = "flux.tailwind"
name = "Tailwind CSS"
version = "0.1.0"
api = "0.4"
authors = ["Egor Ageev"]
description = "Tailwind CSS in Flux: completion of classes with the CSS they make, the CSS of a class on hover, errors in classes and in Tailwind's at-rules, and their quick fixes — from the Tailwind CSS language server."
repository = "https://github.com/egor4geev/flux-plugins"
icon = "icons/tailwind.svg"

# It starts in a project with a `tailwind.config.*` of version 3 (in the root or next to the file's
# `package.json`), or with Tailwind CSS among the dependencies of the file's `package.json` — version
# 4 is configured in CSS (`@import "tailwindcss"`), but its packages (`tailwindcss`,
# `@tailwindcss/vite`, `@tailwindcss/postcss`, `@tailwindcss/cli`) are still dependencies. The server
# then finds the project's configuration itself. Every language id Flux sends is one the server
# knows (`javascriptreact`, `typescriptreact`, `html` for Angular templates): no `includeLanguages`.
[[language-servers]]
id = "tailwindcss-language-server"
command = "tailwindcss-language-server"
args = ["--stdio"]
languages = ["html", "css", "scss", "less", "javascript", "jsx", "typescript", "tsx", "vue", "svelte", "astro", "angular"]
install = { npm = ["@tailwindcss/language-server"], bin = "tailwindcss-language-server" }
secondary = true
activation = { files = ["tailwind.config.*"], dependencies = ["tailwindcss", "@tailwindcss/*"] }

# The answers to `workspace/configuration` (the sections `tailwindCSS` and `editor`), over the
# server's defaults. Emmet's abbreviations are the HTML server's business.
[language-servers.settings.tailwindCSS]
validate = true
emmetCompletions = false
hovers = true
suggestions = true
codeActions = true
classAttributes = ["class", "className", "ngClass", "class:list"]
classFunctions = ["cn", "clsx", "cva", "cx", "twMerge", "twJoin"]
showPixelEquivalents = true
rootFontSize = 16

[language-servers.settings.tailwindCSS.lint]
cssConflict = "warning"
invalidApply = "error"
invalidScreen = "error"
invalidVariant = "error"
invalidConfigPath = "error"
invalidTailwindDirective = "error"
recommendedVariantOrder = "warning"
plugins.readme:
# Tailwind CSS

Tailwind CSS in Flux: completion of classes with the CSS they make, the CSS of a class on hover, errors in classes and in Tailwind's at-rules, and their quick fixes — from the Tailwind CSS language server.

## Files

The files of HTML, CSS, SCSS, Less, JavaScript and TypeScript (with JSX), Vue, Svelte, Astro and Angular templates — the languages their own plugins bring. Classes are found in the `class`, `className`, `ngClass` and `class:list` attributes and in calls of the usual helpers: `cn(…)`, `clsx(…)`, `cva(…)`, `cx(…)`, `twMerge(…)`, `twJoin(…)`.

## Language servers

Flux starts the server when a file of these languages opens in a project with Tailwind CSS: a `tailwind.config.*` file (version 3) in the project's root or next to the file's `package.json`, or `tailwindcss` or a `@tailwindcss/…` package (version 4: `@tailwindcss/vite`, `@tailwindcss/postcss`) among that `package.json`'s dependencies. It runs next to the language's own server and never takes its place: the classes join the language's own completion and hover. If it isn't on the machine, Flux installs it into `~/Library/Application Support/flux/servers` (Settings → Language Servers shows where each one comes from, and installs, updates or removes it).

- **tailwindcss-language-server** (the npm package `@tailwindcss/language-server`) — with a Node.js of Flux's own. It reads the project's Tailwind CSS configuration itself: the `tailwind.config.*` of version 3, or the CSS file with `@import "tailwindcss"` of version 4. Needs Flux 0.4 or later.

# Yandex Tracker

Yandex Tracker in Flux: your tasks on a board, work on a task with its branch and its own tabs, and
your own Claude actions on a task.

## Signing in

**Settings → Plugins → Yandex Tracker → Sign In with Yandex…** — that's all it takes:

- The browser opens Yandex ID's page; once you allow access, it comes back to Flux on this Mac and
  says you're signed in. Flux asks for Tracker's rights and who you are, and — if you allow it — for
  the list of your organizations. Flux keeps the token.
- Flux then finds your organization by itself: one is taken, several are offered to choose from;
  if it can't find any (you declined the list, or the organization is in Yandex Cloud), it shows where
  the ID is — Tracker → Administration → Organizations — and asks for it. Then it checks the
  connection, and the page says who you are and which organization Tracker works in.
- **Change Organization…** — another organization of yours, or an ID by hand.
- While Flux waits for the browser, a notification has **Cancel**; if the browser doesn't come back
  in a while, it suggests the other ways.

**Other Ways…** — when the browser sign-in doesn't suit you:

- **OAuth token** — if you already have a Yandex ID token with `tracker:read` and `tracker:write`.
- **IAM token** — for a federated account of Yandex Cloud: `yc iam create-token` gives one; it lives
  12 hours, then Flux asks for a new one.
- **Own app** — when your organization allows only its own Yandex ID app: its ClientID, and what it
  is for. An app "for user authorization" signs in in the browser (it needs the redirect URIs
  `http://127.0.0.1:52580/callback`, `:52581/callback` and `:52582/callback`); an app "for API access
  or debugging" shows a code in the browser — paste it into Flux.

A new sign-in replaces the previous one; **Sign Out** forgets it. Flux renews the token before it
expires when Yandex allows; when it can't — or Yandex stops accepting the token — a notification
offers to sign in again.

## Tasks

The **Tracker** window on the right (its icon in the launchpad):

- **The list**: My Tasks (the query of the settings), Following, a queue's open tasks or a query of
  your own — the menu at the top; tasks grouped by status.
- **The card** of a task (a double click, ↵, a link): the key and the title; the status — click it for
  its transitions; type, priority, assignee, deadline, sprint, the parent task — and after them every
  other field the task has, as Tracker's own page lists them: the system fields (start and end,
  estimates and time spent, versions, the QA engineer, the project, the epic…) in Tracker's order,
  then the queue's own fields, named as Tracker names them (**Fewer Fields** keeps only the main
  ones). Click a field with ▾ to change it: a person, a date, one value of a list, a line or a number.
  Then the description; **Links** grouped by relation (subtasks, blocks, depends on, relates…), each opens its card;
  **Comments** with a field for a new one (⌘↵ sends) and **History** — who changed what, from what to
  what.
- **A button per Claude action** of the settings. An action sends Claude its prompt with the task's
  data in it: `{key}`, `{summary}`, `{description}`, `{url}`, `{status}`, `{type}`, `{priority}`,
  `{assignee}`, `{author}`, `{queue}`, `{deadline}`, `{sprint}`, `{parent}`, `{branch}`, `{links}`,
  `{comments}`. An action marked **Take the task to work first** does it in one click, as **Take to
  work** in the settings says: moves the task to In Progress, checks out its branch (an existing one
  whose name starts with the key, or a new one by the branch template), switches to the task's tabs,
  starts its timer — then Claude gets the prompt. The action marked **On the board** is the board's
  button. Two come with the plugin: Take to Work and Plan (plan mode).
- **Discuss with Claude**: a new Claude session with the task attached; you write what to do.

**The task in work** is in the status bar — `TRACK-142 · 0:42` — with a timer counted while Flux
runs; its menu: Show, the actions, Log Time…, pause, Close…, Open in Browser. While a task is in work
the commit message starts with it (the commit template of the settings). **Close** logs the time (the
timer's, editable: `1h 25m`, `1ч 25м`, `85m`, `1.5h`), moves the task, switches back to the branch
and the tabs from before the task.

**Open Task** (⌥⇧N) finds a task by its key or words; **⌥⇧B** opens the task in the browser.

Task keys of your queues — `TRACK-142` — are links in the editor (⌘-click; a hover tells the title,
the status and the assignee), in commit messages and in Claude's chat; a click opens the card.

Every few minutes (the settings say how often) the plugin checks for news: tasks newly assigned to
you, status changes of your tasks, and tasks where you're summoned — a notification with Open.

## The board

**Tracker: Open Task Board** opens the board of tasks as a tab among the editor's tabs, as boards
are in Tracker: the board's columns side by side, each with the tasks in its statuses — the key
and the title, the type and the assignee, the priority unless it's the usual one; the task you're
working on is marked ▶. A task in a status no column takes goes to a last column, Other statuses,
rather than out of sight. A scrum board shows its current sprint; a board made of a filter (a queue,
tags) shows what the filter finds.

- **The board** — the menu in the toolbar lists your boards: your favorite boards first, then all
  the others by name. ☆ next to it makes the shown board a favorite. The tab opens the board you
  chose last — at first, your first favorite, or the most recently changed board.
- **Filters**, as on Tracker's boards: **Only mine**, then **Assignee**, **Type**, **Priority**,
  **Tags** and **Components** — each lists the values the board's tasks have, with how many tasks
  show if you choose it; choose one, then another (the menu stays open, Esc closes it): several values
  of one filter show any of them, the filters together narrow each other. The field in the toolbar
  filters by words of the key or the title. A column says how many of its tasks show — "2 of 5";
  × clears the filters. Each board keeps its filter until you change it.
- **Saved filters** — save the current filter of a board under a name and choose it later from the
  same menu (or delete it there).
- **Take to Work** — the favorite Claude action of the settings (the one marked On the board; its
  name is the button's) on the selected task: it moves the task, makes its branch, opens its tabs
  and hands Claude the prompt, as the settings say.
- A task opens in the Tracker window on the right with a double click or ↵.
- The board refreshes when its tab shows, every two minutes while it shows, and when a task on it
  changes in Flux; ⟳ refreshes it now, the globe opens it in Tracker.
